old: It once named only the wingless young, while a different old word covered anything airborne.
In Old English it meant a chick or fledgling, not a flying creature in general.
It slowly pushed aside "fowl," the older general term, starting in the 1300s.
clues: This everyday name for a large class of animals once meant only the babies of the group, while a different word covered the grown-ups.
Today it names any feathered, egg-laying creature with wings and a beak, from tiny sparrows to soaring eagles, not just the farmyard kind raised for eggs and meat.
Think of the early one that catches the worm. Its old rival, fowl, was once the general word, until the two swapped places in everyday speech.
